desc:
Cut a binary tree into diagonals that run from the upper left to the lower right. The root is on diagonal 0; the right child of a node is on the same diagonal as the node, and the left child of a node is on the next diagonal (one more than the node's diagonal).

Return the array whose entry d is the sum of the values of all nodes on diagonal d, for d = 0, 1, 2, ... up to the last non-empty diagonal. The empty tree gives [].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [8, 3, 10, 1, 6, -1, 14, -1, -1, 4, 7, 13] diagonal 0 holds 8, 10, 14; diagonal 1 holds 3, 6, 7, 13; diagonal 2 holds 1, 4. The answer is [32, 29, 5].
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
Every sum fits comfortably in a 32-bit integer
hints: Every node gets a diagonal number that depends only on its parent's number and on whether it is a left or a right child.
The right child keeps the diagonal of its parent; the left child adds one. Parents come before their children in level order.
Walk the real nodes in array order, pass the diagonal number down to the children, and add each value into sums[diagonal] (extend the list when a new diagonal appears).
editorial: Assign each node a diagonal number: diag(root) = 0, diag(right) = diag(parent), diag(left) = diag(parent) + 1. Then the answer is just the sum of the values grouped by that number. Any traversal that visits a parent before its children can compute the numbers; the level-order array does that for free, so one left-to-right pass with an array of diagonals is enough.

Equivalently, you can imagine following the right chain from the root, then from every node on it going to its left child and following that node's right chain, and so on: each chain is one diagonal. Because every diagonal is reached from the previous one, the diagonal numbers are consecutive and the answer has no gaps. Time and space are O(n).
